Mémoire noire, jeunesse montréalaise – À: Black Memory, Montréal Youth – At Maison d’Haïti, Telling the Story of Slavery to Tell One’s Own
À Saint-Michel, des familles discutent d: In Saint-Michel, families talk about slavery and racism to pass history on to children without crushing them.
Maguy Metellus, Marie‑Denise Douyon, Gab: Maguy Metellus, Marie‑Denise Douyon, Gabriella Garbeau, Houmou and Andjelica Caméus. Photo: Nouri Nesrouche
On m’a assigné ce sujet en dernière minu: I was assigned this story at the last minute, filling in for a colleague, and I jumped at the chance, hoping to discover a Montréal address I didn’t know and to hear voices speaking from the source.
De ce point de vue, la soirée littéraire: From that standpoint, the literary evening “L’esclavage raconté à mon enfant” (Slavery, Told to My Child), held Thursday, February 12 at Maison d’Haïti, delivered on its promise, all the more so because covering this event fits with La Converse’s editorial mission of documenting cultural and community initiatives and staying as close as possible to the lived realities of local communities.
Entre paroles croisées des panélistes, p: Between the panellists’ intersecting voices, an artistic performance, exchanges with the audience and remarks gathered on the side, I came away with a deeper understanding of the issues surrounding the transmission of memory, racism and children’s and youth literature.
<strong>Chaque année, le Mois de l’histo: Every year, Black History Month revives discussions about the slavery and racism experienced by Black communities. But beyond commemorations, one question lingers in families: how do you find the words to talk to children about it without crushing them under the weight of history? In the Saint-Michel neighbourhood, a literary evening devoted to this subject brought together women of African descent, parents and teenagers. Through intimate stories, youth literature and artistic performance, the gathering brought to light the silences, the tools and the gestures of care through which a community tries to give its children roots in the context of immigration.
Dans la salle du Centre des Arts de<l1>: In the hall of the Centre des Arts at Maison d’Haïti, on a Thursday evening in February, teenagers mingle with parents, artists and regulars of the space. On stage, four women of African descent take their seats around a table. The title of the event – L’esclavage raconté à mon enfant – might suggest a formal lecture. Instead, it becomes a dialogue of many voices, shot through with silences, intimate anecdotes and artistic gestures. At the heart of the exchanges: transmission, that fragile thread connecting generations of the Black diaspora.
Sur scène, cinq fauteuils rouges disposé: On stage, five red armchairs arranged in a semicircle stand out against the purple backdrop of the screen, where the title of the roundtable is displayed. The speakers sit at the same height, microphones in hand or notebooks resting on their laps, in a posture of exchange rather than lecture. The warm light heightens the feeling of intimacy, despite the size of the hall.
Autour de la table, les trajectoires dif: Around the table, the trajectories differ. Marie‑Denise Douyon is an author and illustrator, known for her visual and editorial work. Gabriella Garbeau is an author, publisher and bookseller. Houmou, a poet and literary critic, leads writing workshops for racialized youth in Quebec City. Andjelica Caméus, who arrived from Haiti as a teenager, takes part in a mentorship program for young women. Their ages, accents and migration experiences vary, but one question keeps coming back: how do you talk to your children about racism and slavery, and when?
Les réponses se construisent par couches: The answers are built in layers. Gabriella Garbeau says motherhood changed the way she sees things. “Becoming a mom, it was like putting on a new pair of glasses,” she confides. She speaks of “umbrella themes,” such as strength, resistance and creativity – so many doorways into harder realities. “I want to tell my children that their story doesn’t begin with a kidnapping,” she sums up, referring to the transatlantic slave trade and the abduction of entire populations, forcibly displaced to North America to serve as slaves. She prefers, she says, to tell young people that Africa, the mother continent, was home to kingdoms, cultures and knowledge that predate the slave trade. Books then become tools, “a toolbox for my children,” that allow conversations to begin.
Houmou, qui a grandi en France, décrit u: Houmou, who grew up in France, describes a blind spot in literature for teenagers. “There’s a lot for kids, a lot for adults, but very little for teens,” she observes. On social media, she therefore showcases works by authors of African descent to fill that gap. She also recounts visiting<l1> Gorée Island</l1> in Senegal, a formative moment in her understanding of slavery; a history, she says, that was rarely passed on within her own family, which was “more inclined toward the positive than toward the pain of memory.”
Andjelica Caméus, elle, parle d’un silen: Andjelica Caméus, for her part, speaks of a different kind of silence. Born in Haiti, where she was raised until age 13, she says she grew up in an environment where skin colour did not structure social relations the way it does here. “Before coming here, I knew absolutely nothing about racism,” she says. It was only when she arrived in Quebec that she became aware of it. She recounts an incident at a library in Saint-Léonard, where an elderly woman accused her of “invading America.” She did not tell her parents right away, out of a reflex of reversed protection, so as not to worry them or reopen old wounds. Silence, in this case, is not forgetting: it is a defence mechanism.
Cette idée revient aussi chez Marie-Deni: The idea also comes up with Marie-Denise Douyon, who explored it further in an interview with La Converse after the roundtable. In her view, transmission is not necessarily opposed to silence; it can sometimes work around it or delay it. The author identifies three realities she has observed in families shaped by exile or migration. First, the silence of the parents themselves, often tied to lives marked by war, dictatorship or genocide, and to a desire to protect children from memories that are too heavy. Second, the question of age: not every story can be told at the same time, and some require greater emotional maturity. Finally, the reverse phenomenon, in which the child keeps quiet about experiences of discrimination so as not to hurt their parents. In every case, she says, it is not a refusal to pass things on, but an adjustment. “It’s more of a protective mechanism”, she sums up.
Pour Marie-Denise Douyon, cet équilibre: For Marie-Denise Douyon, this balance remains essential, because “knowing where you come from in order to know where you’re going” is, in her view, an identity foundation that helps young people face discrimination and find their place in societies where they are often perceived as minorities.
La littérature jeunesse apparaît comme u: Children’s and youth literature emerges as a privileged terrain for these conversations. Marie-Denise Douyon presents her picture book La traversée de Manmzèl Gougousse, in which slavery is told through the character of a mongoose torn from her forest. The choice of an animal, she explains, is meant to avoid stigmatization and shift the gaze. The metaphor makes it possible to approach the transatlantic slave trade without giving human faces to caricatures inherited from colonial history. The story evokes fear, but also dignity and hope.
De son côté, Gabriella Garbeau évoque so: For her part, Gabriella Garbeau discusses her book Grann et moi, l’été de mes 11 ans, the story of a preteen confronted with prejudice about Haiti at school and invited by her father to discover the country for herself. The journey acts as a counter-narrative to dominant media images. Both works share the same concern: offering young people narrative anchors to find their place.
Avant et après la discussion, la danse f: Before and after the discussion, dance echoes the reflection. Choreographer Shérane Figaro and her daughter, performer Aurélie Ann Figaro, present a piece blending classical, contemporary and Haitian traditions. From the start, dance appears as a vehicle for memory and transmission. Slow, restrained gestures give shape to an intergenerational dialogue, illustrating the passing on of knowledge, mentorship and cultural continuity.
Le public, silencieux et attentif, sembl: The audience, silent and attentive, seems suspended on every gesture, every fold of the dancers’ bodies. There is a silent communion: eyes follow the movements the way one follows a story, and breathing seems to fall in with the hybrid rhythms of the stage. At the end, a murmur of admiration gives way to sustained applause, a sign of the deep resonance between the artists and those watching them.
Plusieurs participantes soulignent l’imp: Several participants stress the importance of community spaces. For Andjelica Caméus, “Maison d’Haïti is truly a pillar”, and walking through its door meant “coming home.” She says she was able to talk there about delicate situations she didn’t dare raise with her family, including the risks of using the Internet. Cheers of “bravo” ring out in the room, notably for the staff member who knew how to listen to young Andjelica. For her part, Houmou, who lives in Quebec City, notes the absence of comparable infrastructure in her city and the grounding effect such spaces can have on young people searching for bearings.
In the audience, a mother takes the microphone. Her son, now an adult, only understood the racist nature of certain experiences years after living through them. Time, she suggests, sometimes brings out the words that were missing in the moment. This delayed timeline runs through the whole evening: telling is less about “saying everything” than about “opening a path.”
Au fil des interventions, la transmissio: As the speakers go on, transmission appears less as a duty of memory than as a tool for inhabiting the present. In a context where young Black people often grow up between several cultural references, access to a plural history (African, Caribbean, diasporic) helps consolidate their identity. The speakers do not evade the pain, but refuse to let it be the only way in. They favour gradual approaches: youth literature, metaphors accessible to children, age-appropriate discussions, artistic performances and intergenerational exchanges. The goal is not to water down history, but to make it understandable without making it overwhelming.
Plus qu’un événement littéraire, la renc: More than a literary event, the gathering leaves the impression of a moment of community, a space where people talked about history, but above all about belonging. In this simple, generous warmth, transmission no longer looks like a lesson: it becomes an ordinary, almost familial gesture that carries on well after the last words.

Before the first questions are even asked, host Maguy Metellus grabs everyone’s attention with a call drawn from Haitian oral traditions. “Yé mistikrak!” the room answers in unison. No, the yard is not asleep! With her deep, measured voice, Ms Metellus sets a mood of attentive listening and lays out the context: the Biennale des femmes artistes afro-descendantes, a space designed for creation, encounters and dialogue between artistic practices. In the room, several young Black people have come as a group. The event is explicitly aimed at them.
